newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish Islamist Erbakan faces secularist setback.
newsitem.headline: Turkish Islamist Erbakan faces secularist setback.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, who on Sunday called for new polls to solve a government crisis, is a longtime political outsider locked in an apparently losing battle with the secularist elite.
At a news conference on Sunday with his secularist deputy Tansu Ciller, Erbakan championed the achievements of their 11-month-old coalition but conceded that an election was the only solution.
"We decided that for Turkey to continue its economic success, an early election would be necessary," Erbakan said.
"We believe that we (the coalition partners) will come back stronger if we go to elections."

Since taking office one year ago as modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, Erbakan's unlikely coalition with conservatives has been locked in a bitter political war of attrition with secularists over his plans for Islamist reforms.

But the resolve shown in his chequered 28-year political journey to power, long obstructed by opposition from secularists and political rivals, suggests the veteran Welfare leader could emerge stronger from fresh polls.

Erbakan capitalised on disarray in the secularist political establishment to win a narrow victory in 1995 general elections. Personal rivalries across the spectrum opened the way for his coalition with pro-Western Tansu Ciller, who had been Turkey's first woman prime minister.
Many voters were drawn by his promise of an economic revival and a pledge to raise Turkey's international profile.
He repeatedly espoused a vision of global Moslem brotherhood, going against the grain of Turkey's decades-long ambitions to get closer to Europe and the United States.
"The West learned everything it knows from the Moslems," he said in a newspaper interview before coming to office.
Erbakan visited Iran and Libya shortly after taking power -- in trips that angered Turkey's Western allies.
Statements made by Erbakan subsequently reinforced concerns about his stated hostility to NATO and the European Union.
"The new world leader Turkey will receive the respect and treatment which it deserves," he told his party faithful.

But Erbakan has remained powerless to prevent a blossoming of defence links between Turkey and Israel, sought by the Turkish military, that has drawn anger from Welfare supporters as well as many in the Arab world and Iran.
His resilience has helped him withstand a constant stream of hostility from the secularist media, which he blames for unseating the government by targeting him with "false agendas".
Last month a prosecutor called for the constitutional court to outlaw Erbakan's Welfare Party on grounds that it threatens Moslem-but-secular Turkey's basic principles of state.

"It has become clear that (Welfare) has become a focus of actions contrary to the principle of secularism in the constitution and has pushed our country towards a civil war atmosphere," said charges read out by prosecutor Vural Savas.
The prosecutor cited a warning from Erbakan that Welfare's rise to power could be "bloody" and a call for Moslems to join the party's Jihad (Holy Struggle).
The 70-year-old Erbakan, who served as deputy prime minister in two coalition governments in the 1970s, had managed to fight off a series of censure motions in parliament.

His secularist coalition partner was seen as a major factor in preventing Erbakan from implementing the Islam-based theories, distilled during long years in opposition and spelled out in a manifesto called the "Just Order".

Political and economic realities have undone manifesto vows to scrap interest rates, do away with "world imperialism and Zionism as well as Israel and a handful of champagne-drinking collaborators in the holding companies that feed it".

His plans to build the Developing Eight, an economic cooperation group of Moslem countries, have yet to get off the ground. The domestic economy remains mired in deep public deficits and persistently high inflation.
Erbakan, a mechanical engineer, spent two years doing research at a West German university and factories in the Ruhr during the post-war reconstruction boom.
His time abroad did not distract him from his obligations as a Moslem -- he says he has prayed five times a day since the age of 13. Nor was he impressed with the ways of the West.

He was born in the northern town of Sinop in 1926, one of six children of a father who had served as a travelling Islamic judge in the crumbling Ottoman Empire at the beginning of the century. Erbakan is married with three children.

He entered politics as an independent Islamist MP for the conservative city of Konya in 1969, accusing then prime minister Suleyman Demirel, now president, of removing him as head of a respected business group because of his beliefs.
